concept.technique_name: solving a linear function equation for its input

examples.problem_statement: f(x) = 2x - 3 and f(m) = -11. Quantity A: the value of m. Quantity B: half the value of f(m). Compare the two quantities.

solution.description: Plug m into the rule f(x) = 2x - 3 and set the output equal to the given value -11, turning the function statement into a linear equation.
Add 3 to both sides to clear the constant term and leave the m-term alone on the left.
Divide both sides by 2 to isolate m, which is the value Quantity A asks for.
Quantity B is defined as half of f(m), and the problem states f(m) = -11, so halve -11 to get Quantity B.
Compare the two values on the number line: -4 lies to the right of -5.5, so Quantity A is greater.

key_reminders: f(m) = -11 means substituting m into the rule produces -11, so 2m - 3 = -11.
Quantity B uses the output f(m) = -11, not the input m.
For negative numbers, the one closer to zero is the greater one.
common_mistakes: Halving m (-4) instead of f(m) (-11) when building Quantity B.
Treating -5.5 as greater than -4 because 5.5 exceeds 4 in absolute value.

concept.technique_name: units digit of a factorial sum and of its powers

solution.result: every term from 5! onward contributes 0 to the units digit
solution.description: Note that each factorial from 5! upward contains the factors 2 and 5, so it ends in 0; all those terms can be dropped when only the units digit is wanted.
Add and subtract only the surviving terms 1!, 2!, 3! and 4! with their given signs to get the units digit of N.
Since N ends in 1, raising it to any power leaves the units digit unchanged, so N^N also ends in 1.

key_reminders: Any factorial 5! or higher ends in 0, so it never affects a units digit.
A number ending in 1 keeps units digit 1 under every positive power.
common_mistakes: Attempting to evaluate the full alternating factorial sum instead of truncating at 4!.
Dropping the alternating signs and computing 1 + 2 + 6 + 4 for the leading terms.

concept.sub_category: approximate values in addition and subtraction

solution.description: The answer choices are spread far apart, so round each value to the nearest ten; the first value is rounded up and the second rounded down so the two errors offset.
Work in units of ten: add the two rounded known values as tens, giving 409 tens.
Subtract that total from the right-hand side expressed in tens to find the missing value in tens.
Multiply back by 10 to return the missing value to ordinary units, matching choice 1.

key_reminders: Approximate only as coarsely as the spread of the answer choices allows.
Round one addend up and another down so the rounding errors cancel.
Small changes in the last rounded value do not shift the answer when the choices are far apart.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the tens-scale result 134 back by 10.
Rounding both known addends in the same direction so the errors accumulate instead of cancelling.
